stem: A company buys a machine for USD 500,000 and incurs freight of USD 20,000, installation of USD 30,000, testing of USD 10,000, and staff training of USD 15,000. The amount capitalised is:

explanations.A: Correct. Costs directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition necessary for operation are capitalised: 500,000 + 20,000 + 30,000 + 10,000 = USD 560,000. Training is expensed because the entity does not control the resulting benefit.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 575,000 improperly capitalises the training cost.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 500,000 omits the directly attributable freight, installation, and testing.

stem: Subsequent expenditure on an existing asset is capitalised when it:

options.A: restores the asset to its previously assessed standard of performance.
options.B: enhances the future economic benefits beyond the originally assessed standard of performance.
options.C: exceeds a fixed percentage of the asset's carrying amount.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Routine repairs and maintenance that merely restore expected performance are expensed.
explanations.B: Correct. Capitalisation requires that the expenditure extend the useful life, increase capacity, or improve output quality beyond what was originally expected.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Capitalisation thresholds are practical materiality policies, not the recognition principle.

stem: A machine costing USD 240,000 with a USD 24,000 residual value and a six-year life is acquired on 1 October. Straight-line depreciation for the calendar year of acquisition is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 36,000 is the full annual charge; the asset was in service for only three months.
explanations.B: Correct. Annual charge = (240,000 - 24,000) / 6 = 36,000; for three months, 36,000 x 3/12 = USD 9,000.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 10,000 omits the residual value from the depreciable base.

stem: An airline carries an aircraft at USD 100 million, of which USD 30 million relates to engines with a 10-year life and USD 70 million to the airframe with a 25-year life. Annual depreciation using component depreciation with no residual value is:

options.A: USD 4.0 million.
options.B: USD 5.8 million.

explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 4.0 million applies the 25-year life to the whole asset.
explanations.B: Correct. 30 / 10 + 70 / 25 = 3.0 + 2.8 = USD 5.8 million. IFRS requires separate depreciation of components with materially different useful lives.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 10.0 million applies the 10-year engine life to the entire aircraft.

stem: Component depreciation is:

options.A: required under IFRS and permitted but rarely used under US GAAP.
options.B: required under US GAAP and prohibited under IFRS.

explanations.A: Correct. IAS 16 requires separate depreciation of each significant part with a different useful life or consumption pattern; US GAAP allows it but practice generally depreciates the asset as a whole.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The requirement runs the other way.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neither framework prohibits it.

stem: A company disposes of equipment with a carrying amount of USD 120,000 for cash proceeds of USD 95,000. The income statement effect is:

options.A: a loss of USD 25,000.
options.B: a gain of USD 95,000.
options.C: no effect until the cash is reinvested.

explanations.A: Correct. Gain or loss on derecognition equals proceeds less carrying amount: 95,000 - 120,000 = USD -25,000.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Proceeds are not a gain; only the excess over carrying amount would be.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Derecognition is recognised immediately on disposal.

stem: Average accumulated expenditure on a qualifying asset under construction is USD 4,000,000 and the appropriate capitalisation rate is 6%. Interest capitalised for the year is:

options.B: USD 0.

explanations.A: Correct. 4,000,000 x 6% = USD 240,000, added to the carrying amount of the asset rather than charged to interest expense.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Capitalisation is mandatory, not optional, for qualifying assets under both frameworks.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 4,240,000 is the expenditure plus interest, not the interest itself.

stem: Capitalising interest rather than expensing it will, in the year of capitalisation:

options.A: increase net income and increase reported interest coverage.
options.B: decrease net income and decrease reported interest coverage.

explanations.A: Correct. Interest expense is lower, so EBIT-based coverage looks stronger and profit is higher — which is why analysts add capitalised interest back to interest expense before computing coverage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both effects run the other way.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The classification directly changes reported interest expense.

stem: Under US GAAP, costs of internally developed software are capitalised:

options.A: from the start of the project.
options.B: once technological feasibility has been established.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Costs incurred before feasibility is established are research-like and expensed.
explanations.B: Correct. US GAAP provides a specific exception to the general expense-as-incurred rule for software, using technological feasibility as the trigger.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Software is the main US GAAP exception permitting capitalisation of development costs.

stem: Under IFRS, the six criteria for capitalising development costs include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: technical feasibility of completing the asset.
options.B: the intention and ability to complete and use or sell the asset.
options.C: approval of the capitalisation by the external auditor.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Technical feasibility is one of the required criteria.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Intention and ability to complete, plus the ability to measure the expenditure reliably, are required.
explanations.C: Correct. The auditor forms an opinion on the resulting statements but is not part of the recognition criteria.

stem: Under IAS 36, goodwill is tested for impairment:

options.A: only when an indicator of impairment exists.
options.B: at least annually, at the cash-generating unit level to which it has been allocated.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Indicator-based testing applies to most assets, but goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles require an annual test regardless of indicators.
explanations.B: Correct. Goodwill generates no independent cash flows, so it is allocated to CGUs and tested at that level.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Goodwill cannot be tested in isolation.

stem: An impairment loss recognised for a cash-generating unit is allocated:

options.A: first to goodwill, then pro rata to the other assets of the unit.
options.B: first pro rata to all assets, then to goodwill.
options.C: entirely to the asset with the largest carrying amount.

explanations.A: Correct. IAS 36 requires goodwill to absorb the loss first; only any excess is allocated pro rata across the unit's other assets, subject to floors at each asset's recoverable amount.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Goodwill is the residual and takes the first loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Size of carrying amount is not the allocation basis.

stem: Which of the following is an indicator that an asset may be impaired?

options.A: An increase in market interest rates that materially affects the discount rate used in value in use.
options.B: An increase in the asset's expected useful life.
options.C: An increase in the company's share price.

explanations.A: Correct. IAS 36 lists rising market rates among the external indicators, since they reduce value in use.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A longer life extends benefits and is not an impairment indicator.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A rising share price, if anything, is evidence against impairment; a market capitalisation below net assets is the relevant indicator.

stem: Under US GAAP, the impairment test for a long-lived asset held and used is:

options.A: a single-step comparison of carrying amount to fair value.
options.B: a two-step test: recoverability using undiscounted cash flows, then measurement of the loss as carrying amount less fair value.
options.C: a comparison of carrying amount to the higher of fair value and value in use.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A single-step fair value test would trigger impairments that the US GAAP recoverability screen filters out.
explanations.B: Correct. If undiscounted expected cash flows exceed carrying amount, no impairment is recognised at all, regardless of how far fair value has fallen.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The recoverable-amount concept is the IFRS approach.

stem: Because US GAAP uses undiscounted cash flows in the recoverability screen while IFRS uses discounted amounts, US GAAP impairments will generally be:

options.A: recognised less often but potentially larger when recognised.
options.B: recognised more often and smaller.

explanations.A: Correct. The undiscounted screen is a high hurdle, so fewer assets fail it; once failed, the loss is measured to fair value, which can be well below the discounted recoverable amount IFRS would use.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Undiscounted cash flows exceed discounted ones, making the trigger harder to hit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The two models differ in both respects.

stem: A company applying the revaluation model to its PP&E will, relative to a cost-model peer with identical assets, report:

options.A: a lower debt-to-equity ratio and a lower return on assets.
options.B: a higher debt-to-equity ratio and a higher return on assets.
options.C: identical ratios, since the assets are identical.

explanations.A: Correct. Upward revaluation raises both the asset base and equity, so leverage ratios fall while the larger denominators and higher depreciation depress ROA and ROE.
explanations.B: Incorrect. More equity lowers, not raises, debt-to-equity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Identical economics under different measurement models produce different reported ratios — the essence of the comparability problem.

stem: Under the revaluation model, a decrease in fair value below the original cost, where no revaluation surplus exists for that asset, is recognised:

options.A: in profit or loss.
options.B: in other comprehensive income.

explanations.A: Correct. A revaluation decrease is charged to profit or loss except to the extent it reverses a surplus previously recognised in OCI for the same asset.
explanations.B: Incorrect. OCI absorbs a decrease only up to any existing surplus for that asset.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Direct charges to retained earnings are reserved for error corrections and specified transfers.

stem: Gross PP&E is USD 6,000, accumulated depreciation is USD 2,400, and annual depreciation expense is USD 400. The average age of the asset base is:

options.A: 6 years.
options.B: 9 years.

explanations.A: Correct. Average age = accumulated depreciation / annual depreciation expense = 2,400 / 400 = 6 years.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 9 years is the average remaining life, net PP&E divided by annual depreciation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 15 years is the estimated total useful life, gross PP&E divided by annual depreciation.

stem: An analyst observes that a company's ratio of capital expenditure to depreciation has been below 0.6 for four consecutive years. This most likely indicates:

options.A: the company is underinvesting relative to the consumption of its asset base.
options.B: the company is expanding aggressively.
options.C: the company has adopted the revaluation model.

explanations.A: Correct. Spending less than the depreciation charge means the asset base is shrinking in real terms, which typically flatters near-term cash flow at the expense of future capacity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Expansion would produce a ratio well above 1.0.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The measurement model does not determine the level of capital spending.

stem: Under IFRS, an intangible asset acquired in a business combination is recognised separately from goodwill if it:

options.A: arises from contractual or legal rights, or is separable from the entity.
options.B: was recognised on the acquiree's own balance sheet.

explanations.A: Correct. The identifiability criterion is met by either separability or contractual/legal origin, which is why customer contracts and brands are recognised in an acquisition even though they could not be recognised if internally generated.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prior recognition by the acquiree is irrelevant; internally generated intangibles it could not recognise are recognised by the acquirer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Useful life affects subsequent measurement, not identifiability.

stem: Which expenditure would most likely be expensed rather than capitalised?

options.A: Replacing the roof of a factory, extending the building's useful life by ten years.
options.B: Routine annual servicing of production machinery.
options.C: Legal fees to register a newly acquired patent.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A roof replacement that extends useful life is a capital improvement.
explanations.B: Correct. Routine maintenance preserves rather than enhances the originally expected level of performance, so it is a period expense.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Directly attributable legal costs of securing the asset are capitalised.

stem: A company reduces the estimated residual value of its fleet from USD 20 million to USD 5 million with no change in useful life. The effect is to:

options.A: increase future annual depreciation expense.
options.B: decrease future annual depreciation expense.

explanations.A: Correct. A lower residual value enlarges the depreciable base, so the remaining carrying amount is written off over the remaining life at a higher annual rate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A smaller residual means more, not less, to depreciate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is a change in estimate, applied prospectively.

stem: A company that consistently reports gains on the disposal of its fixed assets is most likely:

options.A: depreciating those assets too rapidly relative to their economic consumption.
options.B: depreciating those assets too slowly.

explanations.A: Correct. A systematic pattern of disposal gains means carrying amounts are consistently below realisable value, which points to overly short useful lives or understated residual values.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Too little depreciation would leave carrying amounts high and produce disposal losses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Revaluation would move carrying amounts toward fair value, eliminating systematic gains.

stem: Under IFRS, an entity choosing the cost model for investment property must nonetheless:

options.A: disclose the fair value of the property.
options.B: revalue the property every three years.

explanations.A: Correct. IAS 40 requires fair value disclosure even under the cost model, so the analyst can adjust for the difference.
explanations.B: Incorrect. No periodic revaluation is required under the cost model.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Classification follows the use of the property, not the measurement model.

stem: Property that a company holds to earn rental income is classified as:

options.A: investment property.
options.B: property, plant, and equipment.

explanations.A: Correct. IAS 40 defines investment property as property held to earn rentals or for capital appreciation, rather than for use in production or for sale in the ordinary course of business.
explanations.B: Incorrect. PP&E is owner-occupied property used in operations.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Property held for sale in the ordinary course of business is inventory, which is the classification for a property developer.

stem: An impairment loss on a finite-lived intangible asset will affect future periods by:

options.A: reducing future amortisation expense.
options.B: increasing future amortisation expense.

explanations.A: Correct. The written-down carrying amount is amortised over the remaining life, so the annual charge falls — one reason a large impairment tends to flatter subsequent reported margins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A smaller base cannot produce a larger charge over the same remaining life.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amortisation is computed on the post-impairment carrying amount.

stem: Which disclosure would help an analyst estimate the timing of a company's future capital expenditure requirements?

options.A: The effective tax rate reconciliation.
options.B: The PP&E note showing gross cost, accumulated depreciation, and useful lives by asset class.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The tax reconciliation explains the tax charge, not asset age.
explanations.B: Correct. Cost, accumulated depreciation, and useful lives by class allow the analyst to estimate average age and remaining life, and hence when major replacement spending falls due.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Share-based compensation concerns employee remuneration.

stem: A company acquires land and a building for a single price of USD 5 million. For accounting purposes the price must be:

options.A: allocated between land and building based on relative fair values, with only the building depreciated.
options.B: assigned entirely to the building and depreciated in full.
options.C: assigned entirely to land and not depreciated.

explanations.A: Correct. Land has an indefinite life and is not depreciated, so the split materially affects reported depreciation and is an area analysts examine for bias.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This would overstate depreciation by including the non-depreciable land.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This would understate depreciation by treating the building as non-depreciable.

stem: Two otherwise identical companies differ only in that one uses straight-line and the other accelerated depreciation. In the early years, the accelerated-method company will report:

options.A: lower net income, lower total assets, and higher asset turnover.
options.B: higher net income, higher total assets, and lower asset turnover.
options.C: identical net income, since total depreciation is the same.

explanations.A: Correct. Front-loaded depreciation depresses early income and carrying amounts; the smaller asset base mechanically raises turnover, which is why turnover comparisons require a depreciation-policy check.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Accelerated depreciation reduces early income and assets.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Total depreciation over the asset's life is the same, but its distribution across years is not.

stem: The most appropriate depreciation method for an asset whose economic benefits are consumed in proportion to output is:

options.A: straight-line.
options.B: units of production.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Straight-line assumes benefits are consumed evenly with the passage of time.
explanations.B: Correct. IAS 16 requires the method to reflect the expected pattern of consumption; where that pattern tracks output, units of production is the faithful choice.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Accelerated methods assume benefits are consumed fastest early in the asset's life.

stem: A company's goodwill balance has grown to 45% of total assets following a series of acquisitions. The primary analytical concern is that:

options.A: goodwill must be amortised, depressing future earnings.
options.B: a large portion of the asset base has no independent cash-generating ability and is exposed to a non-cash but reputationally significant write-off.
options.C: goodwill cannot be tested for impairment.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Goodwill is not amortised under either IFRS or US GAAP.
explanations.B: Correct. Goodwill represents the premium paid over identifiable net assets; a large balance means acquisition prices are largely unsupported by separable assets, and impairment would confirm that value was overpaid for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Goodwill is tested annually at the CGU or reporting-unit level.

stem: When an asset is reclassified from owner-occupied PP&E to investment property measured at fair value, any increase in carrying amount at the date of transfer is:

options.A: recognised in profit or loss.
options.B: treated as a revaluation under IAS 16, with the increase generally in OCI.
options.C: ignored until the property is sold.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Routing the whole increase through profit or loss on a mere reclassification would allow gains to be recognised at will.
explanations.B: Correct. IAS 40 requires the IAS 16 revaluation rules to be applied up to the date of transfer, so the increase generally goes to OCI as a revaluation surplus; fair value changes after the transfer go to profit or loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fair value model requires remeasurement at the transfer date.

stem: An analyst comparing the asset intensity of two companies should be most alert to:

options.A: differences in the age of the asset base, since older assets carry lower book values.
options.B: differences in the companies' fiscal year-ends.
options.C: differences in the number of reportable segments.

explanations.A: Correct. A heavily depreciated asset base produces a small denominator and flattering turnover and return ratios, even when the two companies deploy identical physical capacity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Year-end differences matter for seasonality but not for asset intensity per se.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Segment count is a disclosure characteristic, not a driver of asset intensity.

stem: Under IFRS, the reversal of an impairment loss on a finite-lived intangible asset is limited to:

options.A: the amount of the original impairment, without regard to depreciation.
options.B: the carrying amount that would have been determined had no impairment been recognised.
options.C: the asset's current fair value, with no cap.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This ignores the amortisation that would have accumulated in the intervening periods.
explanations.B: Correct. The reversal restores the asset only to its depreciated historical cost, never above.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An uncapped write-up to fair value is the revaluation model, not an impairment reversal.
